title: Sum of arithmetic sequences
competency: Find the sum of the first n terms of an arithmetic sequence.

ideas.name: Sum of the first n natural numbers

en.text: Write the sum forwards and backwards and add: every pair makes n + 1, and there are n pairs. So twice the sum is n(n + 1), and 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2.

am.text: ድምሩን ወደፊትና ወደኋላ ጽፈን ስንደምር እያንዳንዱ ጥንድ n + 1 ይሆናል፤ n ጥንዶች አሉ። ስለዚህ 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2።

screens.title: Gauss at school
screens.ask: Young Gauss added 1 + 2 + 3 + … + 100 in a few moments. What is the sum?
screens.after:
Pair the ends: 1 + 100 = 101, 2 + 99 = 101, …, 50 + 51 = 101.
100 numbers make 50 pairs.
50 × 101 = 5050.
(10100 counts every number twice; 5000 forgets the extra 1 in each pair.)

screens.why:
Step 1: n = 99, so n + 1 = 100.
Step 2: 99 × 100/2.
Step 3: halve the even number: 99 × 50 = 4950.
Check: 5050 − 100 = 4950 ✓.

en.text: For an arithmetic sequence Sₙ = (n/2)[2A₁ + (n − 1)d]. When you know the first and last terms, use Sₙ = n(A₁ + Aₙ)/2: the number of terms times the average of the ends.

am.text: የአሪትሜቲክ ቅደም ተከተል ድምር Sₙ = (n/2)[2A₁ + (n − 1)d] ነው። የመጀመሪያውንና የመጨረሻውን ተርም ካወቅን Sₙ = n(A₁ + Aₙ)/2።

screens.title: Pairing again
screens.ask: 5, 15, 25, …, 95 has 10 terms. What is the sum?
screens.after:
Pair the ends: 5 + 95 = 100, 15 + 85 = 100, 25 + 75 = 100, …
10 terms make 5 pairs.
5 × 100 = 500.
(1000 counts each pair twice.)

screens.title: Theorem 1.3
paras: Also Sₙ = n(A₁ + Aₙ)/2, where Aₙ is the last term.
The second form is useful when the first and last terms are known.

screens.title: Explore Sₙ = (n/2)[2A₁ + (n − 1)d]
screens.ask: Move A₁, d and n. See the last term and the sum.
screens.note: Both forms always agree. A₁ = 4, d = 5, n = 40 gives 4060.

screens.title: Where the formula comes from
steps: Collect the n copies of A₁: Sₙ = nA₁ + d[1 + 2 + … + (n − 1)].

screens.ask: Use Sₙ = (n/2)[2A₁ + (n − 1)d] with A₁ = 4 and d = 5: S₄₀ = ___
Use Sₙ = (n/2)[2A₁ + (n − 1)d] with A₁ = 30, d = −5, n = 12: S₁₂ = ___
screens.why:
Step 1: n/2 = 6; 2A₁ = 60; (n − 1)d = 11 × (−5) = −55.
Step 2: S₁₂ = 6(60 − 55).
Step 3: 6 × 5 = 30.
So S₁₂ = 30. (The later terms are negative, so the sum is small.)

Arithmetic series in a word problem: the sum of the integers from 1 to 100 divisible by 10 is ___
screens.why:
Step 1: the numbers are 10, 20, …, 100: an arithmetic sequence with d = 10.
Step 2: count: 100 ÷ 10 = 10 terms.
Step 3: S = 10(10 + 100)/2 = 5 × 110 = 550.
screens.clue: How many multiples of 10 are there?

screens.ask: Arithmetic series in a word problem: the sum of the odd integers from 1 to 2001 is ___
screens.why:
Step 1: 1, 3, 5, …, 2001 has d = 2.
Step 2: count: 1 + (n − 1)2 = 2001, so n − 1 = 1000 and n = 1001.
Step 3: S = 1001(1 + 2001)/2 = 1001 × 1001.
Step 4: 1001² = 1 002 001.
Check: the sum of the first n odd numbers is n² ✓.
screens.clue: First find how many odd numbers there are: 1 + (n − 1)2 = 2001.

screens.ask: Arithmetic series with overlap: the sum of the integers from 1 to 100 divisible by 2 or 5 is ___
screens.why:
Step 1: multiples of 2: 2, …, 100 (50 terms): 50(2 + 100)/2 = 2550.
Step 2: multiples of 5: 5, …, 100 (20 terms): 20(5 + 100)/2 = 1050.
Step 3: multiples of 10 are in both lists: 550.
Step 4: 2550 + 1050 − 550 = 3050.
(Trap: 3600 counts the multiples of 10 twice.)
screens.clue: Add the multiples of 2 and of 5, then take away the multiples of 10 counted twice.

items.why:
Step 1: multiples of 2: 2550.
Step 2: multiples of 5: 1050.
Step 3: subtract the multiples of 10 (counted twice): 550.
Step 4: 2550 + 1050 − 550 = 3050.
items.clue: Do not count multiples of 10 twice.

screens.text: Find a term with Aₙ = A₁ + (n − 1)d: A₁ = 7, d = −2. A₆ = ?
screens.why:
Step 1: n = 6, so there are 5 jumps.
Step 2: A₆ = 7 + 5(−2).
Step 3: 7 − 10 = −3.
Check: 7, 5, 3, 1, −1, −3 ✓.
